country.comment: Primary empirical data were collected in two urban informal settlements (Korogocho and Viwandani) in Nairobi, Kenya (Section 2.1 notes the broader ARISE Consortium spans Kenya, Sierra Leone, India and Bangladesh, while this study's empirical fieldwork is exclusively in Nairobi, Kenya).
country.where_found: PDF p. 2, Abstract; PDF p. 6, Section 2.2; Figure 1; Table 1, PDF p. 7

effect_estimate.comment: Purely qualitative thematic study with no quantitative point estimates or inferential statistics.
effect_estimate.value: Qualitative — no numeric effect estimate reported. Informal self-governance practices (aligned with Ostrom's common-pool resource principles) fill formal governance gaps in service provision across Korogocho and Viwandani: structure owners lock water points and toilets for paying users (boundary definition), water vendors organize into mutual-support groups, providers negotiate flexible payment schedules and operating hours, and communities use collective meetings, user monitoring, graduated sanctions (service denial, repayment or eviction) and low-cost third-party/negotiated conflict resolution; however, water and sanitation access is undermined by unclear government policies and pricing guidelines (causing non-use or debt at public toilets), inflexible bureaucracies, overlapping responsibilities, lack of transparency and service delays (long queues at water and sanitation points), political interference and landowners withholding plot space for public facilities.
effect_estimate.where_found: PDF pp. 2–3, Abstract; PDF pp. 9–17, Sections 3.1–3.3; Tables 3–4, PDF pp. 9, 12

mechanism_certainty.comment: Primary qualitative interview study appraised with CASP (design ceiling = 2). Directly documents through interviews with water/sanitation providers and local leaders how informal rules and formal governance gaps (boundary locking of water points and toilets, flexible fee/schedule accommodations, unclear pricing policies, landowner plot refusals, bureaucratic rigidity, sanctions and participatory meetings) operate on water and sanitation access.

mechanism_flags.comment: Examines structure/plot ownership and landowner refusal to allocate space for public facilities (property, planning), payment rules for locked water points/toilets and unclear public toilet pricing causing debt (fees), rigid bureaucracies and lack of timely information on service delivery stages causing delays (procedural_steps, delay), informal local negotiations over flexible payment schedules and service hours (accommodation), community collective-choice and consultation forums (participation), graduated sanctions including service denial and eviction (sanction), reporting vandalism/closures and disputes to chiefs, police or third parties (complaint), overlapping responsibilities and unclear policies across government tiers (institutional_fragmentation), and politician support vs. interference in service delivery (political_coordination).
mechanism_flags.value: ELIGIBILITY, BURDEN, DISCRETION_ACCOMMODATION, ENFORCEMENT, property, planning, fees, procedural_steps, delay, accommodation, participation, sanction, complaint, institutional_fragmentation, political_coordination
mechanism_flags.where_found: PDF pp. 9–17, Sections 3.1–3.3; Tables 3–4, PDF pp. 9, 12

outcome_flags.comment: Examines user access to water points/kiosks and shared/public toilets (water_access, sanitation_access), flexible payment negotiations vs. unclear public toilet charges causing non-use or debt (affordability), service quality impacts of boundary setting and clear policies (service_quality), uncertain or closed facility operating hours (service_continuity), and service delivery delays and long queues at water and sanitation points (delay).
outcome_flags.value: water_access, sanitation_access, affordability, service_quality, service_continuity, delay
